title: Segregation in Washington and New York until World War II
summary: Greer says Washington and Harlem restaurants and stores were segregated until the war; no trying on hats.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: No, go ahead. Ask your question.
It seemed like you had something in your mind.
No, I can come back to it.
You say Washington was a segregated city.
Oh, yeah. New York was segregated. Right on 125th Street, restaurants, you couldn't go in and sit down and eat, you know. I know that for a fact because I done it, and that was -- the heart of it.
You say that the City of Washington itself, the racial prejudices didn't break down until --

The second World War, because they was bringing government workers and different people working with government from all over the United States, so naturally they had to break down, because the colored was working down there The chick? was down wasn't no colored people go downtown in Washington and sit in no restaurant, go in a store and buy a hat. You couldn't go in there and buy a suit. I mean, try it on, you couldn't try no shoes on, hats, because my wife she wasn't used to that.
And a friend of mine, Fizol's wife, say they ain't going to let you try on no hat. My wife --
So if you tried them on they would tell you you had to buy it.
You buy it. You do this, you done bought that one, whether it fits you or not. You bought that.
